extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers of natural philosophy and evolutionary theory (19th-century scientific audience)
extracted.subtask_description: A conceptual rubric for identifying and distinguishing Evolution as a general process across natural, social, and cultural domains; explains which kinds of change count as Evolution and which do not. The page supplies criteria (heterogeneity, definiteness, integration/dissipation) plus many illustrative examples from music, literature, geology, embryology, society, and species-formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance from the homogeneous to the heterogeneous
rubrics_metrics.description: Evolution is characterised by 'the advance from the homogeneous to the heterogeneous' — a change from simpler, more uniform forms to more complex, variously differentiated forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained with examples across arts and sciences: dancing, poetry, and music separating from religion and from one another; musical instruments multiplying and producing greater heterogeneity of melody, modes, keys, time, and orchestral complexity; literature, science, architecture, drama, and the press developing many divisions and subdivisions. The text stresses that heterogeneity appears as multiplication of unlike parts (genera, species, forms) and cites contrasts between 'aboriginal music' and 'modern music' to illustrate the increase in heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolution as change from the indefinite to the definite
rubrics_metrics.description: Along with increased complexity, Evolution involves a passage 'from the indefinite to the definite' — an advance from confusion/undetermined arrangement to order/determined arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to distinguish Evolution from mere disordering changes: embryological development (primitive streak → definite tube/vertebral canal), planetary formation (nebulous matter → defined spheroids/planes), geological settlement (thin crust → fixed continents and oceans), and social evolution (wandering tribes → nations). Definiteness is shown by increasingly specific outlines, settled spatial relations, and precise internal structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accompanies dissipation of motion and integration of matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Evolution 'accompanying the dissipation of motion and integration of matter' — the general formula tying physical processes to developmental change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book defines Evolution (in fuller phrasing) as 'a change from an incoherent homogeneity to a coherent heterogeneity, accompanying the dissipation of motion and integration of matter.' This anchors the conceptual criteria in physical/thermodynamic-like processes (concentration/settlement of matter and reduction of chaotic motion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous integration (concentration) and differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evolution involves both integration (progressing concentration of the aggregate) and simultaneous differentiation (its parts becoming unlike one another).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as parts growing more 'distinct' while the whole integrates — e.g., the Earth's crust thickening (integration) while producing mountains, rivers, and distinct strata (differentiation); in organisms, organs become distinct while the organism as a whole integrates into a coherent body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterogeneity must be determinate (distinctness) — not mere disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every increase of heterogeneity is Evolution: to count as Evolution the increased heterogeneity must be accompanied by increased definiteness (order); changes that increase multiformity but destroy definiteness (indefinite multiformity) are not Evolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit counterexamples: morbid growths, decomposition of a dead body, social disorders (rebellion, dearth causing bankruptcies, riots) and earthquakes — these increase heterogeneity but produce indeterminate, confused, or disorganising changes. The text contrasts determinate heterogeneity of development with indeterminate heterogeneity of disease/dissolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness evidenced by precise locality, proportion, form, and internal structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Definiteness is shown by regularity and specificity in position, size, form, proportions, and internal organization; organs/species in true development have constant relations and clear outlines unlike morbid or decomposing parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: organs vs morbid growths (organs have constant proportions and specific forms; tumors are variable and indefinite); embryology (blastoderm → primitive streak → vertebral canal; heart developing distinct receiving/propelling portions); species (higher organisms show precise proportions and constant structures compared to Protozoa). These markers are used to judge whether a change is determinate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive settlement of spatial and force relations (planetary/geological examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: In physical evolution (nebular/planetary, geological), Evolution is indicated by progressive settlement of spatial relations (e.g., planes of rotation, oblateness reduction) and force relations becoming more definite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: nebulous matter forming an oblate spheroid with a single plane of rotation; planets' axes becoming less subject to disturbance as form solidifies; Earth's crust thickening enabling fixed continents, clearer river systems and sedimentary strata. These constitute physical evidence of increasing definiteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolutionary increase of heterogeneity manifests as proliferation of distinct genera/species/forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Across biological and cultural domains, Evolution can be recognised by the multiplication of distinct kinds — many genera, species, musical forms, literary forms, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text cites enumeration of music's many genera and species (vocal, instrumental, mixed; hymn, chant, canon, motet, oratorio; ballad, serenata, symphony), literature's divisions, and sciences' diversification. The proliferation of well-differentiated categories is used as evidence of Evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embryological and ontogenetic markers of Evolution: increasing definiteness step-by-step
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual development (embryology) exemplifies Evolution via stepwise increases of definiteness: indistinct cell masses become organs with distinct walls, cavities, ducts, and functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete embryological stages cited: peripheral cells forming blastoderm; germinal area and area pellucida; primitive trace → vertebral canal; intestine becoming a tube by infolding; heart developing distinct chambers and septa; lungs developing from buds. These developmental sequences serve as diagnostic evidence of true evolutionary (progressive, determinate) change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergence and disappearance of intermediate forms (natural selection implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: When species arise by accumulation of modifications (natural selection), Evolution involves divergence making contrasts between groups greater and disappearance of intermediate, less well-adapted forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text refers to Darwin's account: 'tendency to divergence, causing the contrasts between groups to become greater' and notes disappearance of intermediate varieties leads to distinct and stable species. This criterion links evolutionary mechanism (selection) to the observed increase in definiteness and distinctness of groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness can increase after heterogeneity growth ceases (ageing/ridigity as non-progressive definiteness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase of definiteness may continue even when heterogeneity no longer increases; such later definiteness (e.g., rigidity with age) can be maladaptive and lead to decline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: human articular surfaces finishing into sharp epiphyses by age ~30; later-life modifications making structure too precise and narrow in tolerance, restricting adaptability and contributing to old age and death. The text warns that definiteness without appropriate adaptive heterogeneity can be deleterious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing Evolution from Dissolution: presence of ordered, determinate arrangement vs indeterminate change
rubrics_metrics.description: A working criterion to separate Evolution from dissolution is whether the change produces ordered, determinate arrangement (Evolution) or indeterminate, disorganising heterogeneity (Dissolution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to social examples: earthquake or revolution may make a city more multiform but less orderly — an increase of heterogeneity that is indeterminate and thus a step toward Dissolution rather than Evolution. The distinction is central to correctly classifying observed increases of complexity.
